841.title: Lohgarh and the Gurus' coins
841.hook: Banda strikes coins and seals in the name of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh
841.tomorrow: Land to those who work it
841.howItsDone: Sikhs remember that Banda Singh Bahadur struck coins and a seal at Lohgarh in the names of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh rather than his own, and the words deg and tegh are still used for the Khalsa's twin duty to feed and to protect.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a field outside Sirhind, and an ending that arrived but couldn't give back what was lost. Your line was it came. Who did you remember who's still waiting? Today, something small enough to hold in your palm. Day eight hundred forty-one.

Take a coin out of a pocket or a purse and turn it over. There's usually a name on it, or a face, or a seal: whoever claims the right to say this metal is worth something. A coin says who rules here. So it means something that once Banda Singh held territory, he made his base in the hills at a fort called Lohgarh, and from there he struck coins and stamped seals. The question is whose name went on them. Today: Lohgarh and the Gurus' coins.
screen: `TURN A COIN OVER.` → `A NAME SAYS WHO RULES HERE.` → `COINS STRUCK AT LOHGARH.`

segments.voice: A coin was one way a new power announced itself. Banda Singh now had a fort, an army and lands under his hand, and he could have stamped his own name. He didn't. Sikh tradition says the coins and the seal were struck in the names of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh. The first Guru and the tenth. Not Banda Singh. Remember the instructions tradition says came with the five arrows: never set yourself up as a Guru, and remember you serve the Khalsa. The coins look like that instruction made into metal. The power was real, but the name on it belonged to someone else. The words on his seal were in Persian, and as Sikh tradition reads them, they speak of deg and tegh. The deg is the cooking pot, the great kettle of the langar where anyone can eat. The tegh is the sword, raised to protect. Pot and sword, side by side, as the gift of the Gurus. It's a short summary of what the Khalsa was meant to be: feed people, and defend them. Some readers hear in these coins the stamp of Sikh rule. Others hear something quieter. A man with every chance to make his own name large chose to stamp the names of his Gurus instead. On an ordinary day, the pull is the same in small ways: the report with our name at the top, the credit we'd like to keep. The coins of Lohgarh point the other way.
screen: `HE COULD HAVE STAMPED HIS OWN NAME.` ·`BANDA SINGH STAMPED THE GURUS' NAMES.` · `DEG AND TEGH: POT AND SWORD.` · `FEED PEOPLE, AND DEFEND THEM.` · then, large: `IN THEIR NAMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a coin. If one is nearby, hold it. If not, picture one. Sit, and let the breath settle. Read what's on it, slowly, side by side. Whose name, whose face, whose words? Then ask what name you'd want stamped on the things you make: your work, your kindness, your choices today. Not your own name necessarily. Maybe someone who taught you. Maybe Waheguru. Hold the coin, or the picture of it, through the sit. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Lohgarh and the Gurus' coins. Banda Singh's fort in the hills, and the coins and seal he struck there in the names of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: in their names. Today, when you finish something good, name the person who taught you to do it, out loud or in your head. Day eight hundred forty-one.

842.title: Land to those who work it
842.word: Land to those who work it
842.hook: Banda breaks the big estates and gives land to the farmers who tilled it
842.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Banda Singh Bahadur for giving land to the farmers who tilled it, and connect it to Guru Nanak's teaching of kirat karni, earning by honest work, told in the story of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago.

segments.voice: Yesterday, coins struck at Lohgarh with the Gurus' names where a ruler's own name would go. Your line was in their names. Whose name did you give credit to? Today, from coins to soil. Day eight hundred forty-two.

Two people stand at the edge of a field. One has mud to the knees; he plowed it, sowed it, and will cut it at harvest. The other has clean hands and a paper that says the field is his, and when the grain comes in, he takes the larger share. Tradition remembers that in Banda Singh's Punjab, land often worked that way. Big landholders collected, and the people who did the work kept what was left. Sikh tradition remembers that where Banda Singh's rule reached, he turned that around. Today: land to those who work it.
screen: `MUD TO THE KNEES.` → `CLEAN HANDS AND A PAPER.` → `BANDA SINGH TURNS IT AROUND.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Banda Singh broke up the big estates in the lands he held and gave the fields to the farmers who actually tilled them. Accounts differ on how far and how long this reached; he held those lands only for a time, under constant attack. But the idea is the part Sikhs keep. To hear where it comes from, go back to the very start of the path, to Guru Nanak. Sikh tradition tells of Guru Nanak staying with a carpenter named Bhai Lalo, a poor man who earned his bread by his own hands. A rich official, Malik Bhago, held a great feast and expected the holy man to come. Guru Nanak stayed with Lalo's plain bread. In the story, when the Guru is pressed to explain, he holds Lalo's coarse bread in one hand and Malik Bhago's rich food in the other and squeezes them. From Lalo's bread comes milk. From the feast, blood, because it was gathered from other people's labor. The Sikh word for that honest labor is kirat. Kirat karni, earning by honest work, is a pillar of Sikh life, taught beside remembering the Name and sharing. Banda Singh's land grants take that story out of a kitchen and into whole villages. The bread belongs with the hands that made it. The field belongs with the hands that work it. Some readers hear a modern echo in it, whenever people argue about who should own the fields they farm. But at its root, the idea is just a carpenter's bread, held up against a feast.
screen: `BIG ESTATES BROKEN UP.` · `LALO'S BREAD AND MALIK BHAGO'S FEAST.` · `KIRAT: EARNING BY HONEST WORK.` · `THE FIELD BELONGS WITH THE HANDS.` · then, large: `LAND TO THE TILLERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a farmer. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of the last thing you ate. Trace it backward, one step at a time: the shop, the truck, the packing shed, and finally a field somewhere, and a person bent over it in the heat or the cold. You'll probably never know their name. Hold them in mind anyway, with their tired back and their dirty hands. Let a simple thank you rise toward them. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out, and remember the hands behind your bread. The bell holds the time.
Land to those who work it. Banda Singh's breaking of the big estates, giving fields to the farmers who tilled them, rooted in Guru Nanak's honor for honest work. Today's word.
screen: `LAND TO THOSE WHO WORK IT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: land to the tillers. Today, at one meal, pause before the first bite and thank the hands that grew it. Day eight hundred forty-two.

843.title: Hunted in the hills
843.hook: Mughal armies pursue Banda through the hills for years
843.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Banda Singh Bahadur's years of being pursued through the hills as a time of chardi kala, ever-rising spirits, a phrase that closes the Ardas said at Sikh gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a carpenter's bread and fields given to the hands that worked them. Your line was land to the tillers. Did you thank the hands behind a meal? Today the tide turns, and the hunt begins. Day eight hundred forty-three.

Night at Lohgarh. The fort in the hills is surrounded. The emperor's army has come north in force, and the walls won't hold much longer. Inside, tradition says, one Sikh makes an offer. He'll put on Banda Singh's clothes and sit where Banda Singh sits, so that when the enemy breaks in, they'll think they have their man. In the dark, the real Banda Singh slips out through the hills with whoever can follow. By morning the fort has fallen, and the man they capture isn't the one they came for. Today: hunted in the hills.
screen: `LOHGARH IS SURROUNDED.` → `A SIKH WEARS BANDA SINGH'S CLOTHES.` → `OUT INTO THE HILLS BY NIGHT.`

segments.voice: That night begins a long stretch of Banda Singh's life that has no grand battles to name it. The Mughal armies kept after him, season after season, through the hills and the jungles at the edge of the plains. He'd vanish, regroup, strike, and vanish again. Lands won were lost. Towns changed hands. The people who sheltered his men paid a price. Sikh tellings don't make this part glamorous. It was cold camps, short food, running at night, and the slow grind of being hunted. What kept them going? Sikhs have a phrase for it that appears at the end of the Ardas, the prayer said at the close of Sikh gatherings: chardi kala. It means something like rising spirits, an ever-ascending spirit. Not cheerfulness. Not pretending things are fine. Chardi kala is the steadiness to keep facing upward when every report is bad. In the Ardas it's paired with a wish for the good of all, which says something about where that spirit is supposed to point. Notice also the man who wore Banda Singh's clothes. Earlier on this path, at Chamkaur, tradition told of a Sikh named Sangat Singh who wore the Guru's plume so the Guru could slip away. Now it happens again. That pattern is its own kind of chardi kala: a willingness to stand in someone else's place so the work can keep going. The hills didn't change the hard news. But one borrowed set of clothes bought one night, and one night was enough to keep going.
screen: `A LONG STRETCH WITH NO GRAND BATTLES.` · `VANISH, REGROUP, STRIKE, VANISH.` · `CHARDI KALA: AN EVER-RISING SPIRIT.` · `SOMEONE STANDS IN YOUR PLACE.` · then, large: `KEEP GOING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep going through a hard week. Sit, and let the breath come and go on its own. Name, quietly, the thing in your week that feels like being hunted: the deadline, the bill, the worry that keeps finding you. Don't fight it. Just let it be named. Then find one small next step, the size of one night's walk in the hills. Not the whole road. One step. Rest your attention on that step and on your breathing. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out, and let the phrase chardi kala sit beside it. The bell holds the time.
Hunted in the hills. The long stretch after Lohgarh fell, when Banda Singh and his men were pursued through the hills and jungles and kept going. Today's word.
Your line: keep going. Today, take the one small step you found in the sit, and only that one, and let it count. Day eight hundred forty-three.

844.title: The siege of Gurdas Nangal, 1715
844.hook: starved in a mud fort for months, Banda's men are finally captured
844.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the siege of Gurdas Nangal, where Banda Singh Bahadur and his companions were starved until they were captured, as an example of sidak, steadfast faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a disguise at Lohgarh and a long hunt through the hills. Your line was keep going. What small step did you take? Today the hunt narrows to one walled place. Go gently with this one. Day eight hundred forty-four.

Mud walls. Not stone, not a fortress on a cliff. A walled compound in a village called Gurdas Nangal, with a ditch around it, and inside, Banda Singh and his people: fighters, and with them families. Outside, an army settles in to wait. Nobody storms the walls. They don't need to. They simply make sure nothing comes in. No grain. No supplies. Tradition says the waiting went on for months. Today: the siege of Gurdas Nangal.
screen: `MUD WALLS AND A DITCH.` → `AN ARMY SETTLES IN TO WAIT.` → `NOTHING COMES IN.`

segments.voice: A siege like this is fought with time and hunger. Sikh tellings describe what happened inside the walls as the food ran out. People ate what grain was left, then the animals, then leaves and grass and the bark of trees. Some tellings go further, and they're hard to hear. They describe people too weak to stand, still keeping their places. Accounts differ on the very end: whether the gate was opened at last, or the army simply walked in on people who could no longer resist. Either way, when hunger had done its work, Banda Singh and the men who were left were taken, worn to almost nothing. The carry is they held on. Not they won. Not they escaped. Sikhs have a word for this: sidak. It means steadfastness, a faith that stays fixed when everything around it gives way. It isn't the same as courage in a charge. Courage can be a single moment. Sidak is a long thing. It's what's left on yet another hungry morning, when nothing heroic is happening and nobody is watching. In Sikh memory, Gurdas Nangal is one of the places where that word was tested hardest. There's a quieter lesson in it too, for a listener whose week has nothing to do with sieges. Much of holding on looks like nothing. It's not leaving. It's getting up again. It's staying where you said you'd stay. That kind of faithfulness doesn't make a good painting, which is maybe why it's worth a word of its own.
screen: `A SIEGE FOUGHT WITH TIME AND HUNGER.` · `GRAIN, THEN LEAVES, THEN BARK.` · `SIDAK: FAITH THAT STAYS FIXED.` · `HOLDING ON OFTEN LOOKS LIKE NOTHING.` · then, large: `THEY HELD ON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of hunger for a minute. Sit, and let the breath settle. Notice your stomach right now: full, empty, somewhere between. Then let your mind rest, gently, on people who are hungry today, near you or far away, who didn't choose it. Don't push for a feeling. Just keep them company in your attention. After a while, come back to the people inside those mud walls, and to the word sidak. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
The siege of Gurdas Nangal. The long siege in which Banda Singh and his people were starved in a walled compound until they were captured, remembered by Sikhs for their sidak. Today's word.

845.title: The march to Delhi, 1716
845.hook: hundreds of Sikhs are paraded and executed daily, and tradition says none renounced their faith
845.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the captives taken to Delhi with Banda Singh Bahadur, of whom tradition says none gave up their faith, and the Ardas remembers those who kept their sikhi to their last breath.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mud walls at Gurdas Nangal, and the long faithfulness called sidak. Your line was they held on. Who did you help toward a meal? Today is a hard day on this path. Take it slowly. Day eight hundred forty-five.

A road from Punjab to the capital, and a procession on it that was meant to be seen. The captives from Gurdas Nangal, Banda Singh among them, were taken to Delhi and paraded through the streets, chained, before crowds. This was a display. The empire wanted everyone watching to understand what happened to people who rose against it. Then came the executions, a group at a time, day after day. And tradition says that every one of the captives was offered the same way out. Today: the march to Delhi.
screen: `A PROCESSION MEANT TO BE SEEN.` → `PARADED, CHAINED, THROUGH DELHI.` → `THE SAME WAY OUT, OFFERED TO EACH.`

segments.voice: The way out was simple. Give up your faith, and live. Tradition says the offer was made, and that not one of them took it. That's the carry: none renounced. Sikhs still tell one story from those days. A mother, tradition says, went to the officials and pleaded for her young son. He isn't really a Sikh, she told them. He was caught up with the others by mistake. And she was granted his release. But when the order reached him, the young man refused it. He said, in the telling, that his mother was mistaken; he was a Sikh, and he would stay with his companions. And he died with them. It's a hard story, and Sikhs don't tell it to make anyone want to die. They tell it because of what it shows about faith that's been chosen, not inherited or assumed. He could have walked out. Nobody would have blamed him. He decided who he was out loud, at the worst possible moment. There's a Sikh word for the whole of that life: sikhi. The Ardas remembers those who kept their sikhi to their last breath, with their hair uncut, which for a Sikh is part of keeping faith whole. The march to Delhi is part of that memory. Today doesn't ask anything heroic of a listener. But it does leave a quiet question behind it. When it costs something small, a raised eyebrow, an awkward pause, do we say who we are, or let someone else say it for us?
screen: `GIVE UP YOUR FAITH, AND LIVE.` · `A MOTHER PLEADS; HER SON REFUSES.` · `CHOSEN, NOT ASSUMED.` · `SIKHI KEPT TO THE LAST BREATH.` · then, large: `NONE RENOUNCED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one minute of silence, and then a little more. Sit upright, the way people stand when a name is read aloud. Let the breath slow. Don't think of the details of what happened in Delhi. Just hold, in silence, the people who were offered a way out and kept their faith instead. If faces come, let them be faces you'll never know. When your mind wanders, return to the silence, as if you were standing in a crowd that has gone quiet. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
The march to Delhi. The captives from Gurdas Nangal, paraded through Delhi and executed day after day, of whom tradition says none renounced their faith. Today's word.
Your line: none renounced. Today, in one small moment where it would be easier to stay quiet about what matters to you, say it plainly and kindly. Day eight hundred forty-five.

846.title: Banda's end
846.hook: Banda is tortured and killed in Delhi, with his young son
846.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Banda Singh Bahadur's death in Delhi, with his young son Ajai Singh, as a martyrdom, and honor him by the name Bahadur, the brave.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the captives in Delhi, offered their lives if they would give up their faith. Your line was none renounced. Where did you say plainly what matters to you? Today the story of Banda Singh reaches its last day. Go gently. Day eight hundred forty-six.

A cot by a river at Nanded. A hermit hurries home, finds a stranger sitting where no one sits, and ends the day calling himself that stranger's banda, his servant. It was only nine days ago on this path. In the story it's years. The servant carried five arrows north, took towns, struck coins in his Gurus' names, gave fields to farmers, ran through the hills, starved behind mud walls, and was marched in chains to Delhi. Now his companions are gone, and his own turn has come. Today: Banda's end.
screen: `A COT BY A RIVER AT NANDED.` → `FROM SERVANT TO PRISONER.` → `HIS OWN TURN COMES.`

segments.voice: Sikh tellings of Banda Singh's last day are hard, and they don't need to be told in full to be understood. He was brought out in Delhi with his young son, Ajai Singh. Tradition says he was offered his life, as the others were, if he would give up his faith, and he refused. Then the hardest part of the telling. Tradition says his little boy was killed in front of him, and that Banda Singh did not break. Then he himself was put to death, slowly, by torture. The tellings dwell less on the pain than on his stillness. Some say an official asked him how a man who had done so much could come to this, and that he answered calmly, speaking of God's will and of how wrongdoers are punished in God's time. The exact words vary, and it's best not to put new ones in his mouth. That's the carry: he did not break. Not that he wasn't hurt. Not that he wasn't afraid. Only that what he'd chosen at that cot by the river stayed chosen to the end. Sikhs remember him by the fuller name, Banda Singh Bahadur, the brave. They remember him in more than one way, too; parts of his story were argued over by Sikhs who came after, and that's a story for tomorrow. But on this day, the memory is simple. The man who began by calling himself a servant ended as one, keeping faith with the One he served.
screen: `BROUGHT OUT WITH HIS YOUNG SON.` · `OFFERED HIS LIFE, HE REFUSES.` · `THE TELLINGS DWELL ON HIS STILLNESS.` · `A SERVANT TO THE END.` · then, large: `HE DID NOT BREAK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light a lamp for the brave. If you have a candle, a lamp, or even a phone light, turn it on and set it in front of you. If not, picture a small flame. Sit, and let the breath slow. Look at the light without staring. Let it stand for the people who didn't break: Banda Singh, his son, the captives in Delhi, and anyone you know of, in any time, who kept faith under pressure. You don't need words. Let the light do the remembering. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Banda's end. The death of Banda Singh Bahadur in Delhi, with his young son, when, tradition says, he refused to give up his faith and did not break. Today's word.
Your line: he did not break. Today, when something presses on you, take one slow breath before you answer it, and stay who you chose to be. Day eight hundred forty-six.

847.title: Two Khalsas, one decision
847.hook: tradition says a split among Sikhs was settled by Bhai Mani Singh casting two slips into the Amritsar pool
847.howItsDone: Sikhs greet each other with "Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh," and tell the story of the two slips at Amritsar as part of the history of the Panth after Banda Singh.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Banda's end. Your line was he did not break. This week walked from coins struck in the Gurus' names, to land for the tillers, to the hills, the siege, the march, and the end. What held for you this week? Day eight hundred forty-seven.

Two slips of paper, folded small. A pool of still water. A crowd on the steps, everyone watching the surface. That is how, tradition says, a bitter argument among Sikhs was settled. Not by a vote. Not by a fight. By two pieces of paper and a wait. After Banda Singh was gone, Sikhs found themselves on two sides of a line over the customs some of his followers had taken up. Both called themselves Khalsa. Both came to Amritsar. Today: two Khalsas.
screen: `TWO SLIPS. ONE POOL.` → `NOT A VOTE. NOT A FIGHT.` → `BOTH CALLED THEMSELVES KHALSA.`

segments.voice: Here is the quarrel, as tradition tells it. Some of Banda Singh's followers had taken up new customs, including a new greeting. Others held that the Guru had given the Khalsa its greeting already, and that nothing should be added. One side came to be called the Bandai Khalsa. The other called itself the Tat Khalsa, the true or essential Khalsa. Both sides had fought and suffered. Neither was a stranger to sacrifice. And when they gathered at Amritsar, the tension was close to breaking into violence. So Bhai Mani Singh, the respected Sikh caring for the Harmandir, proposed a test that neither side could rig. Tradition says he wrote the two greetings on two slips of paper. On one, the greeting the Bandai Sikhs had taken up. On the other, the greeting the Khalsa had used since Guru Gobind Singh, the one this path heard again on the day of Chappar Chiri: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh. Both slips went into the pool together. Whichever floated would be accepted. And everyone agreed to the terms before the slips touched the water. The story says the other slip sank, the Guru's greeting floated, and the matter was settled. Some tellings add more, a wrestling match or a later dispute. But the heart is the same in each: before the outcome, both sides agreed on how they would decide. A fair process is a gift to the side that loses. It lets them walk away without being humiliated. It lets the community stay one community. Sikhs still greet each other with those words today, and the tradition remembers the day a pool of water kept a family from breaking apart.
screen: `A NEW GREETING SPLITS THE PANTH.` · `BHAI MANI SINGH PROPOSES A TEST.` · `BOTH SIDES AGREE FIRST.` · `THE GURU'S GREETING FLOATS.` · then, large: `WAHEGURU JI KA KHALSA, WAHEGURU JI KI FATEH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: settle one quarrel fairly, starting in your head. Sit, and let the breath slow down. Bring to mind one disagreement that is still open, at home, at work, in a group chat. Don't decide who's right. Instead, ask what a fair way of deciding would look like, one that both of you could agree to before you knew the answer. Take turns? Ask someone neutral? Wait a day? Let that fair method take shape in your mind. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Two Khalsas. The Bandai Khalsa and the Tat Khalsa, two sides after Banda Singh, settled, tradition says, by slips of paper in the Amritsar pool. Today's word.
Your line: settle it fairly. Today, in one disagreement, propose the way of deciding before you argue the answer, and keep to it whichever way it goes. Day eight hundred forty-seven.
